title: Stuck on Art&Assets Production After Building a Working Game Prototype. What’s Your Workflow?
author: YoshiBanana3000
selftext:
Hey vibecoders,

I recently got into vibecoding to bring some of my ideas to life, nothing too ambitious, just personal projects.

I’m making solid progress on functional prototypes of small mobile games, but there’s one area where I’d really appreciate your advice: art direction, animations, assets, sound design etc.

For example, I currently have a fully working board game, but it has no sprites, no animations, no sound, no music...basically just the mechanics.

What tools do you use for animations, design, and make it consistent with a art direction ? What does your workflow look like?

I have this feeling that I’m both very close to finishing my project, and at the same time that the art direction is a huge blocking point, and possibly the hardest part ahead.

comments.author: Significant-Neck-520
comments.body:
I'm doing static images, rellying on procedural shaders and procedural animations for the juice, also particle effects. It works for me because it is a card game, but the same could be done for a board game.
Edit: also, this will depend a lot on what you are using for coding. I'm doing things in unity, so there is a lot implemented out of the box.

comments.author: macuseri686
comments.body:
So the main issue with using a standard AI tool like Google Nano Banana or Chat GPT image gen for game assets and sprite sheet animations is that those models can't output transparency, and they have no concept of animation frames. You'll spend more time cleaning up the output than you saved generating it.

https://i.redd.it/ex905sq96q4h1.gif

I actually ran into this enough that I ended up building GameLab Studio [https://gamelabstudio.co](https://gamelabstudio.co) . It handles transparent spritesheets, consistent angles/palette across frames, and tileable textures.

comments.author: ClueHappy324
comments.body:
I ran into the same issue a couple of weeks ago. I decided to pause design and implementation to nail down artistic direction and, more importantly, define a realistic and repeatable asset pipeline. Otherwise, my project was effectively dead.

Currently, AI is excellent at 2d static assets. The issue is 2d animation.

But you know what? AI sucks at 2d animation. But you know what else? 2d animation is really hard for humans, too. 3d has a higher up-front cost (modeling + rigging, *then* you can animate), but after eating that up-front cost, consistency is practically solved. This is precisely why many popular 2d games opted to use 3d models for characters. Ori and the Blind Forest and Dead Cells are great examples. In their case specifically, they model, rig, and animate fully in 3d, but then render animations to a sprite sheet for use in-game.

That's the direction I'm going as well. Image-to-model tech has gotten really, really good. Auto-rigging, at least for bipeds, is really good as well, and otherwise pretty easy to do yourself. Animation is still not solved by AI, but 3d animation is perhaps one area I'd be ok contracting out to an actual expert. In the meantime, Mixamo animations - for bipeds at least - will be sufficient.

If you specifically need 2d animation, the common way with current tech is image-to-video. Have AI generate your 2d asset, say a 2d character. Then have AI (i.e. GPT Image 2) create a video of that 2d character performing your desired action, like running. Then, you'll download that video, and chop it up into frames. You can then use those frames to create your spritesheet. That process can be automated, or watch one of the hundreds of videos out there on how to do exactly this.

replies.author: YoshiBanana3000
replies.body:
Interesting.  
So in short: text to 2D image -> 2D image to 3D -> 3D animation -> capture frames  
Or, text to 2D image -> 2D image to 2d video -> capture frames

replies.author: ClueHappy324
replies.body: Yep. From what I can tell, many AI-focused game devs are going the second route for 2d games specifically.

comments.author: West_Rutabaga3310
comments.body: For fast and easy brainstorming I've liked using [gentube](https://www.gentube.app/p/world-builder?_cid=wb) to map out my worlds and characters; really like that its free and unlimited so you can go crazy making a ton and exploring different concepts

comments.author: Kingnorik
comments.body: I use chat gpt to create sprite sheets. 5x2. Then I go to Photoshop and clean em up. Resize the image to 1280 by 512. Remove the background and add a grid line. Then I center the images into each "frame".
